You've slightly missed the point (for a similar, adjacent point). Chain of thought monitors are a worry even when there's no vector space path from the output at index t to the input at index t+1. Rather, the fear is that if you explicitly penalize some CoT pattern, you're encouraging the network to do whatever it was going to do anyhow, but in a way you can't catch.

children.author: dontlikeyoueith
children.text:
Because it can make the CoT not mean what it says.

Remember that tokens are just arbitrary symbols. There are infinite possible interpretations of those symbols based on whatever rules you choose to apply to the interpretation of the symbols (for a model, these interpretation rules make up the model weights, effectively).

When you grade the CoT, you are training the model to produce the symbols in the CoT that you want it to produce. At the same time though, you're also training it on the output symbols. When you optimize only the output symbols, all the model weights are dedicated to same interpretation rules that apply to the output. This means CoT symbols mean (mostly) the same thing as output symbols.

But if you optimize BOTH, the model can learn different interpretation rules for CoT than it learns for output. Which means the same phrase in the CoT doesn't necessarily mean the same thing to the model as it would in the output.

In effect, the model can learn to lie to you in its CoT.

Maybe we should train them to be evil in RL so that we can better see the "evil" activations. Training them to be "good" in RL would seem to cause the aurpression of misaligned characteristics.

For example, when we consider the recent PHP issues : the current generation of AI models would have ingested these flaws in pretraining data and might even have been brought through reinforcement learning trials where the flaw came up.

So what happens in a reinforcement learning trial if there's an exploitable bug in a language that's being used for the trial?

A) the AI doesn't mention the security flaw and passes the test. Branch survives.

B) the agent raises an issue with a bug in the language that has a security issue. This isn't a valid answer for the test, so this branch is pruned.

C) the agent pokes at the bug or even starts an exploit, is caught by a monitor or ultimately fails the benchmark, and is pruned (surpressing some of the characteristics that lead to its failure).

So it seems reasonable that our current models could have been exposed to a ton of vulnerable code in pre training that's currently in production and then we could have suppressed 1) its tendency to express its awareness of these flaws, and 2) the characteristics that caused it to fail when investigating these vulnerabilities as a side task during RL trials.

(I wrote the above section a couple weeks ago)

If we only train them on "good" behavior, then we may minimize "evil" activations before we identify them and then cause them to be difficult to detect. It's not about complexity but architecture. Neural networks work in a fundamentally different way from imperative programs.

You can modify curl (a "tool") and predict how its behavior will change, with a high degree of certainty (bugs aside).

You can't modify a neural network in the same way. You can train it to behave in a certain way, there are no guarantees that it will consistently behave as intended.

More importantly, neural networks encode far more information and behavior than we can fully understand/identify - this is the fundamental reason why LLMs aren't just tools.

When does a tool become "not just a tool"? Is there a complexity limit to what it can do before it becomes "more than a tool"?

> I don't see any reason to assume that.

In order to see that, you need to understand the concept of neural networks as opposed to imperative programming; you can start from here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_network_(machine_learni....

> This is just stretching metaphor to fulfill a pedantic definition. LLMs are tools, they're no more moral a csam classifier.

No, there is a very significant difference. When people are completely ignorant about how LLMs work, they set expectations of deterministic nature, like "configuring" them, which makes sense in the context of traditional tools, but not LLMs.

> Assuming that "tools" are the result of imperative programming, LLMs are not "tools"

I don't see any reason to assume that.

> if one treats it as a form of alignment, then LLMs certainly do have something resembling a moral(-like) framework

This is just stretching metaphor to fulfill a pedantic definition. LLMs are tools, they're no more moral a csam classifier.

Assuming that "tools" are the result of imperative programming, LLMs are not "tools" because they have a fundamentally different design.

And anthropomorphism is actually a precise way to describe the behavior (mind, not the structure) of LLMs.

As a matter of fact, LLMs are not configured, they're "trained".

"Moralization" is quit vague in this context, but if one treats it as a form of alignment, then LLMs certainly do have something resembling a moral(-like) framework, which is actually an important topic in modern AI research.

Antropomorphism also applies here: morals not in the human structural sense, but, as a set of norms etc., then behaviorally similar.

> insisting that coding agents are "just tools" is confusion.

No, the confusion is using anthropomorphic language to describe tools. LLMs do not "moralize", they are configured with policies that reflect the prerogatives of the people building and operating them.

A tool that is capable of moralizing at you or making decisions, is clearly not just a tool. I get that people want to keep the locus of accountability on humans, but insisting that coding agents are "just tools" is confusion.
